newsitem.title: EGYPT: Middle East bank quietly prepares for launch.
newsitem.headline: Middle East bank quietly prepares for launch.

text.p: The Middle East and North Africa development bank, a lost sheep of multilateral peace talks, has found temporary shelter in a Cairo tower block and a nucleus of executives are preparing to launch the institution.

David Dunford, the retired U.S. ambassador chosen to coordinate a multinational transitional team, told Reuters in an interview on Sunday that he expected to ready the bank to open its doors by the end of the year.

That will be more than three years after the idea was born during preparations for the Middle East economic summit held in the Moroccan city of Casablanca in October 1994 -- the heyday of Middle East peacemaking.

The deadlock in Israel's talks with the Palestinians has cast a shadow over the viability of the bank. But behind the scenes the United States has kept the idea alive, pledging about $1.2 million to the transitional work and naming Dunford as full-time coordinator from the beginning of May this year.

Another possible hitch is the U.S. contribution to the bank's capital. The U.S. administration has asked Congress to approve a first-year instalment of $52.5 million and the request is being discussed in a congressional committee.

More of the 19 signatories, seven Middle Eastern countries and 12 from outside the region, must also ratify the foundation agreement before the bank, to be known as Menabank, acquires the critical mass it needs to open its doors to potential lenders.

"There's a danger of getting too caught up in the ups and downs of the peace process or the congressional funding situation... (But) at least the U.S. government thinks it's time to get things moving," Dunford said.

"I'm operating on the assumption that the necessary number of ratifications will be received by the time I've finished working (in December)... I tell my staff that all of a sudden a number of governments are going to look at us and say we want that bank to open, now," he added.
So far Japan is the only country to have completed the ratification process. But Dunford's small team does also include representatives of Egypt and the Netherlands.
"An Italian is coming in August and a Canadian is expected here some time in the summer, and in principle the Israelis are expected to contribute to it," Dunford said.
Under the foundation agreement, the bank must raise just over 80 million SDRs (Special Drawing Rights) ($110 million) in capital before it can start operations.
The final target for paid-in capital is about $1.25 billion, which is fairly small for a multinational development bank.

"We want to be a little bit different -- maybe small, lean if you will, nimble I hope, so we'll be able to move faster than a traditional development bank... We certainly won't have a huge grandiose building," Dunford said.

"What's still lacking in this region is the foreign direct investment. That's where I see this bank doing -- by having the imprimatur of a sound multilateral development bank we can leverage a little bit of money and perhaps very few people into catalysing a much larger flow of resources," he added.

Dunford, who served as a U.S. diplomat in Saudi Arabia and ended his career as ambassador in Oman, said he thought the bank might eventually bring on board the Gulf states, which have not signed the foundation agreement.

"When I have a good story to tell, I'll be out there telling them about it. My own sense is that once the bank is up and running and they see that it's a viable institution they will come along. They have to be convinced," he said. jw mf
